summary.text: Counting multiples of powers of a prime and using Legendre’s formula gives the numerator and denominator valuations as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\) and \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{c\ge1}c\lfloor m/(cp^i)\rfloor\); the termwise bound \(\sum_c c\lfloor M/c\rfloor\le M^2\) also proves that the denominator divides the numerator, so the quotient valuation is their difference. For \(m=np+k\) with \(0\le k<p\), every relevant floor \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\), and hence \(\lfloor m/(cp^i)\rfloor\), equals its value at \(np\), while all newly introduced tail terms vanish, so both valuations—and therefore their difference—are unchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{r=1}^{m}\gcd(j,r),
\qquad
D(m)=\prod_{c=1}^{m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac m c\right\rfloor!\right)^c.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)},
\]
where the quotient is taken in the integers. We will prove along the way that \(D(m)\mid N(m)\), so this quotient is indeed exact.

For a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(x\). We first derive formulas for the \(q\)-adic valuations of \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\).

For any positive integer \(x\),
\[
v_q(x)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid x},
\]
where \(\mathbf 1_E\) is \(1\) if the condition \(E\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Also, among \(1,2,\ldots,m\), exactly \(\lfloor m/d\rfloor\) integers are divisible by \(d\). Since all integers occurring below are at most \(m\), it is harmless to truncate every sum over \(i\) at \(i=m\): all later terms vanish. (A much smaller bound would also suffice.)

For positive \(j,r\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))=\min(v_q(j),v_q(r)).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\min(v_q(j),v_q(r))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j\ \text{and}\ q^i\mid r}
\]
when \(j,r\le m\). Therefore, by additivity of valuations on products and by interchanging finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\min(v_q(j),v_q(r))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}
   \mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid r}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid r}\right)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]

We next calculate the denominator valuation. Legendre's formula gives, for every nonnegative integer \(s\),
\[
v_q(s!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{s}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
For completeness, this follows by writing \(s!=\prod_{t=1}^s t\), replacing each \(v_q(t)\) by \(\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid t}\), interchanging the sums, and counting the multiples of \(q^i\) up to \(s\). Here again, when \(s\le m\), the sum may be truncated at \(i=m\).

Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{c=1}^{m}c\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mc\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{c=1}^{m}c\sum_{i=1}^{m}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/c\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{c=1}^{m}
 c\left\lfloor\frac{m}{c q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
The last equality uses the elementary nested-floor identity
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/c\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{c q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]

We now show that \(D(m)\mid N(m)\). Fix a prime \(q\) and an index \(i\), and put
\[
M=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Again by the nested-floor identity,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{c q^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac Mc\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(c>M\), the latter quantity is zero. Hence
\[
\sum_{c=1}^{m}c\left\lfloor\frac{m}{c q^i}\right\rfloor
=\sum_{c=1}^{M}c\left\lfloor\frac Mc\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(1\le c\le M\),
\[
c\left\lfloor\frac Mc\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
There are \(M\) such terms, so
\[
\sum_{c=1}^{m}c\left\lfloor\frac{m}{c q^i}\right\rfloor
\le M^2
=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Summing (3) over \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and using (1) and (2), gives
\[
v_q(D(m))\le v_q(N(m))
\]
for every prime \(q\). Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive: every factorial is positive, and every gcd in \(N(m)\) is positive because its arguments lie between \(1\) and \(m\). The prime-factorization criterion for divisibility therefore yields
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\tag{4}
\]
Thus \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is a positive integer, and exactness of the quotient gives
\[
a(m)D(m)=N(m).
\]
Taking the \(q\)-adic valuation yields the basic identity
\[
v_q(a(m))+v_q(D(m))=v_q(N(m)).
\tag{5}
\]

We now fix a positive integer \(n\), a prime \(p\), and an integer \(k\) with
\[
0\le k<p.
\]
Set
\[
m_0=np,\qquad m_1=np+k.
\]
We will show separately that the \(p\)-adic valuations of both \(N\) and \(D\) agree at \(m_0\) and \(m_1\).

The elementary floor fact driving both arguments is that, for every \(i\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, division by \(p\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
= rac{np}{p},
\]
because \(0\le k<p\). Dividing this common quotient successively by the remaining factor \(p^{i-1}\), or equivalently using the nested-floor identity, proves (6).

Apply formula (1), first with \(m=m_1\). By (6), every summand with \(1\le i\le m_1\) can be changed from
\(\lfloor m_1/p^i\rfloor^2\) to \(\lfloor m_0/p^i\rfloor^2\). The terms whose indices satisfy \(m_0<i\le m_1\) are zero. To see this, note that \(p\ge2\), and for every positive integer \(i\), one has \(i<2^i\le p^i\). Since \(m_0<i\), it follows that \(m_0<p^i\), so \(\lfloor m_0/p^i\rfloor=0\). Thus the sum may be shortened from \(i\le m_1\) to \(i\le m_0\), giving
\[
v_p(N(m_1))
=\sum_{i=1}^{m_0}\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
=v_p(N(m_0)).
\tag{7}
\]

We next prove the corresponding denominator equality. Formula (2) says
\[
v_p(D(m_1))
=\sum_{i=1}^{m_1}\sum_{c=1}^{m_1}
 c\left\lfloor\frac{m_1}{c p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{8}
\]
We first show that all outer-sum terms with \(i>m_0=np\) vanish. For such an \(i\), we claim that
\[
m_1=np+k<p^i.
\tag{9}
\]
Because \(n\ge1\), we have \(p\le np\). Since \(k<p\), this gives
\[
np+k<2np.
\]
For the positive integer \(np\), the standard inequality \(np<2^{np}\) gives
\[
2np<2^{np+1}.
\]
Since \(p\ge2\),
\[
2^{np+1}\le p^{np+1}.
\]
Finally, \(i>np\) implies \(i\ge np+1\), and hence
\[
p^{np+1}\le p^i.
\]
Combining these inequalities proves (9). For every \(c\ge1\), (9) implies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m_1}{c p^i}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Therefore (8) reduces to
\[
v_p(D(m_1))
=\sum_{i=1}^{m_0}\sum_{c=1}^{m_1}
 c\left\lfloor\frac{m_1}{c p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{10}
\]

For each remaining \(i\ge1\), equation (6), followed by division by \(c\), gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m_1}{c p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor m_1/p^i\rfloor}{c}
\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor m_0/p^i\rfloor}{c}
\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{c p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{11}
\]
Substituting (11) into (10),
\[
v_p(D(m_1))
=\sum_{i=1}^{m_0}\sum_{c=1}^{m_1}
 c\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{c p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{12}
\]
If \(c>m_0\), then \(c p^i\ge c>m_0\), so the corresponding summand in (12) is zero. We may therefore shorten the inner sum from \(c\le m_1\) to \(c\le m_0\). Formula (2) at \(m_0\) then gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(m_1))
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m_0}\sum_{c=1}^{m_0}
 c\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{c p^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=v_p(D(m_0)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

Finally, apply identity (5) with \(q=p\) at \(m=m_0\) and \(m=m_1\):
\[
v_p(a(m_0))+v_p(D(m_0))=v_p(N(m_0)),
\]
\[
v_p(a(m_1))+v_p(D(m_1))=v_p(N(m_1)).
\]
By (7), the right-hand sides are equal, and by (13), the denominator-valuation terms are equal. Cancelling that common term gives
\[
v_p(a(m_0))=v_p(a(m_1)).
\]
Recalling \(m_0=np\) and \(m_1=np+k\), we have proved
\[
\boxed{\ v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k))\ }
\qquad(0\le k<p).
\]
Since this holds for every \(k=0,1,\ldots,p-1\), all the values
\[
v_p(a(np)),\ v_p(a(np+1)),\ldots,\ v_p(a(np+p-1))
\]
are equal, as claimed.
